newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S., France freeze moves to solve command row.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France freeze moves to solve command row.

text.p: The U.S. and France have dropped attempts to resolve a long-running dispute over command of NATO's strategic southern flank, part of a troubled wider reform of the alliance's outdated command structures.

Paris had been pushing for command of NATO's southern flank, AFSOUTH, at Naples to be taken out of U.S. hands and given to a European and had linked the issue to the wider question of a full return to NATO's military wing.

Briefing reporters on a plane taking him to a NATO ministers' meeting in Brussels, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said the issue had been deferred following the election of a Socialist-led government in France headed by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

The French socialists have strongly criticised President Jacques Chirac for abandoning France's policy of trying to create a separate European defence identity and leading the country back into the military wing of the U.S.-led military pact it quit in 1966.
"I think that as a result of the elections, much of that (AFSOUTH) discussion has simply been deferred. I'm not aware of any discussions recently," Cohen said.
In Paris, Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told reporters that Franco-American negotiations on the issue "have at least temporarily stopped".
She said Chirac would have to discuss the issue with Jospin before France took a final position on whether to return fully into NATO's military wing.
"It's a decision they will take together," she said.

Chirac has pushed for the creation of a greater role for Europeans within an expanded North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as part of a restructing to enable it to carry out more Bosnia-style missions outside its traditional area.

In parallel with the French-U.S. stand-off over AFSOUTH, NATO ministers have failed to make much progress on reforming the alliance's Cold War structures to make it flexible enough to accept new members.

The alliance is due to invite certain countries from former communist Europe to join at a special summit in Madrid on July 8-9. It was orginally hoping to adopt the new command structure and announce France's full participation at the same summit.

On Thursday, the U.S. said it wanted only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be asked to join, dealing another blow to hopes of resolving the row with France which had supported a broader enlargement to include Slovenia and Romania.
"France has no incentive to come back in, at least in the short-term, and no cards to play with it if it does not. The whole thing is on ice for a while," said one NATO official.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana tried to put a brave face on NATO's apparent failure to meet its own timetable.
"The internal reform of NATO will not be finalised by Madrid, but will be by the end of the year," Solana told a news conference.

He added he believed the new French government "is going to continue on the same line" as the last on integrating into the new military structure, but declined to say whether that would also be done by the end of the year.

After a meeting with new French Defence Minister Alain Richard, he said he was unsure whether talks on France's reintegration would restart before a July 8-9 summit in Madrid to invite former enemies to join a new NATO.
"Whether they are resumed or not is an open question at the moment," Cohen said, adding that he found his new French colleague "warm and engaging."
"He (Richard) did say that he wanted the issue resolved one way or the other prior to Madrid and I think that is a positive proposal," Cohen told reporters.
Richard told reporters that the French government felt there was room for a better rebalancing between Europe and the United States in the new command structure, but that progress had been made.
